title: BigQuery Compute Costs: Fix the Configuration Before You Fix the Queries
body_markdown:
*Written By:*[Sajad Bhat](https://www.linkedin.com/in/sajad-bhat-aa3962275/)


BigQuery compute and storage together were consuming 65–70% of our entire GCP bill. Our instinct was to look at this problem where it was most visible: the queries themselves.


So we built observability first. We created dashboards that track slot consumption and average slot usage per hour and per day, broken down by project and across the overall workload. Alongside that, we built a query cost dashboard pulling from job history metadata, showing the total cost incurred by each query and the average cost per run.


The turning point came when we overlaid slot utilization against our reservation configuration. The chart told a clear story: our baseline was sized for an earlier workload, so routine, predictable demand was regularly spilling into autoscale every day. We weren’t overspending because of bad queries. We were overspending because the infrastructure underneath was configured for a workload pattern we didn’t have.


When we dug further, we found more configuration drift. Slot reservations still reflected our initial setup and hadn’t yet been revisited as the workload grew. Materialized views were refreshing hundreds of times a day against tables that were rarely, if ever, queried. The real money was hiding in configuration, not code.


The biggest wins came from settings that made sense at the start but hadn’t been revisited as our workload changed. We started with the change that had the biggest impact and required zero code, even though it meant proposing a higher commitment to reduce the bill.


### Right-Sizing Slot Reservations


This was the change that felt the most counterintuitive when we proposed it: increasing committed capacity to reduce cost.


To see why spending more saved us money, the pricing mechanics matter. We had configured a baseline (the minimum number of slots always allocated to the reservation). We had configured a baseline, which is the minimum number of slots always allocated to the reservation. We pay for these slots whether they’re in use or not, but commitments on baseline slots can usually be purchased at a discounted rate. Pairing a baseline with a commitment lets you lock in a lower rate for the capacity you know you’ll consume.


On top of the baseline, we set an autoscale ceiling. BigQuery provisions additional slots on demand when the workload exceeds the baseline. Autoscale slots are always billed at the PAYG rate, with a one-minute minimum and are billed for allocated slots, not used slots.


The original configuration reflected a conservative, cost-conscious setup: a low baseline of 1,800 slots and a generous autoscale ceiling of 10,000. The logic was “only pay for what we use.” In practice, this configuration cost more than needed for our workload profile because our demand was predictable, not spiky. The “base load” (the slot demand present almost every hour) was well above the 1,800-slot baseline. So every day, predictable, routine work was spilling into the autoscale tier.


The internal conversation wasn’t easy. Proposing a 122% increase in committed capacity to reduce the bill looks wrong on a slide: the commitment line goes up, and you’re asking leadership to trust that the autoscale line comes down by more. We had to lead with the utilization data, not the proposal: show the pattern first, let the math make the case, and only then present the recommendation.


According to the official[Google pricing](https://cloud.google.com/bigquery/pricing#capacity-compute-pricing) , the one-year commitment rate is roughly 20% cheaper per slot-hour than the autoscale PAYG. We were paying a flexibility premium for capacity we were going to use anyway.


We analyzed nearly six months of hourly consumption data across percentiles. The 90th percentile sat around 4,000 slots. We increased the baseline from 1,800 to 4,000, a 122% increase in committed capacity, to reduce total compute cost. Those 2,200 additional slots shifted from the PAYG autoscale rate to the commitment rate, resulting in a 20% per-slot-hour reduction in the capacity we were consuming regardless.


Simultaneously, we lowered the autoscale max from 10,000 to 9,000. A high ceiling doesn’t just mean capacity to burst; it means permission to burst. Without backpressure, queries happily consumed whatever was available. Lowering the ceiling forced us to be intentional about which workloads genuinely needed burst capacity and which could queue. We brought it down in phases, monitoring for queuing or increased query latency at each step.


The result: roughly 15% annual savings on slot reservations.


The “feels wrong” moment was proposing a higher level of commitment to leadership as a cost-reduction measure. For workloads with predictable baselines, on-demand isn’t flexibility; it’s a premium we pay for capacity we were going to use anyway.


Right-sizing isn’t a one-time exercise. Workloads change as pipelines get deployed and retired. We set up a weekly check to compare actual slot utilization against the configuration.


With reservations accounting for the largest single reduction, two other compute optimizations stacked on top — each meaningful on its own, but deliberate in sequencing.


### Other Compute Wins That Stacked on Top


#### 1. Rethinking Materialized View Refresh Intervals


Materialized views are meant to save money by precomputing expensive aggregations, so downstream queries hit a cached result instead of reprocessing raw data every time. In practice, the MVs were costing more in slot consumption than the query savings they delivered. This fix accounted for 7% of the total BQ spend reduction.


BigQuery’s default MV refresh interval is five minutes. That interval suits near-real-time data needs. It is very costly when the base table is queried only a handful of times a day. Each refresh consumes slot-seconds and rewrites data, and the cost scales with both the number of MVs and the size of their base tables.


We audited every MV in the project and found dozens refreshing more than 200 times per day against tables that were queried once a day, or not at all.


One of the most extreme cases was an MV that aggregated about 1 TB of data. It was built on a 19.5 TB base table with 6.4 billion rows, and it used the default five-minute refresh interval. That meant 288 refreshes per day. We checked the last 90 days of job metadata: three queries per day on average, with some days as low as one. The view was refreshed 288 times to serve three reads.


We moved the view from a five-minute to a six-hour refresh interval with a matching max_staleness of six hours, dropping from 288 to four refreshes per day. That’s 284 daily query refreshes against a 19.5 TB base table, each consuming slots, scanning partitions and rewriting results that no downstream consumer would read before the next refresh overwrote it. Over a month, that’s over 8,500 wasted refreshes eliminated from a single view.


Now multiply that across the dozens of other MVs we found with similar profiles. The fix wasn’t to turn off MVs; it was to align refresh frequency to actual consumption patterns. We cross-referenced MV refresh logs with downstream query frequency and bucketed every MV into three categories:


**High-frequency consumers** (operational dashboards, live monitoring): kept at aggressive refresh intervals, typically one to three hours.


**Low-frequency consumers** (daily batch reads, periodic analyst queries): moved to three- to twelve-hour refresh intervals.


**Zero consumers dropped** these MVs entirely. They had been built for pipelines that were later retired, so their consumers were gone while the views kept running as configured. They continued to refresh on schedule, using slots to produce results that no one read.


Tuning refresh intervals, aligning staleness tolerance with actual downstream query frequency and dropping orphaned MVs resulted in up to a ~90% reduction in compute cost for MV-related slot consumption. The effort was entirely configuration: no SQL rewrites, no pipeline changes. Just ALTER MATERIALIZED VIEW … SET OPTIONS (max_staleness = INTERVAL ‘6’ HOUR, refresh_interval_minutes = 360) and a few DROP MATERIALIZED VIEW statements for the defunct ones. Only after these configuration-level wins were in place did we turn to the work that most teams start with– the SQL itself.


#### 2. Reducing Slot Waste in Existing Queries


We made SQL changes last, after the infrastructure and configuration changes described above had already lowered the baseline. SQL optimization was the second-largest category, at 10% of total BQ spend savings. It was also the highest-effort category, because every SQL fix requires engineering time, testing, and deployment.


We pulled the top queries by total slot-hours consumed over 90 days. Those top queries, out of hundreds running daily, accounted for roughly 90% of total slot consumption. The patterns were well-documented BigQuery anti-patterns.


Google’s own[query optimization documentation](https://docs.cloud.google.com/bigquery/docs/best-practices-performance-compute) guide covers query-level best practices, and we applied them to these queries. The specific fixes are not the main point; profiling by slot-hours told us which queries mattered, and we deliberately sequenced this highest-effort work after the configuration changes that needed no SQL or pipeline changes.


### Takeaways


Three changes: reservation right-sizing (~15% on slot costs), MV refresh tuning (7% of BQ spend) and targeted SQL fixes (10% of BQ spend), together accounted for the largest share of the compute cost reduction. But the order matters more than the individual fixes.


We deliberately worked lowest-effort-first. The reservation restructuring and MV tuning were configuration changes: no code, no tests, no deployments, no risk of breaking a pipeline. SQL optimization came last because it required engineering time for every improvement. By the time we got to query rewrites, the infrastructure wins had already lowered the baseline and the SQL fixes stacked on top, compounding the savings.


If your BigQuery compute bill is growing, and your first instinct is to start rewriting queries — pause. Check the reservation configuration. Check whether the baseline covers steady-state demand or whether you’re paying autoscale rates for a predictable load. Check whether materialized views are refreshed hundreds of times a day for tables nobody is querying. The most expensive line in the BigQuery bill might not be a bad query. It might be a default you never revisited. We didn’t discover a better way to optimize SQL. We discovered we’d been solving the wrong problem first. The queries were never the biggest cost driver. The infrastructure they ran on was.
